This is deliberate institutional ‘conflation’ not lazy analysis,” argued a trader. “There was less SAAS shorting and even some covering in the last couple of weeks but I'm pretty sure we will see that go up next several sessions until NOW reports next week. Could be an inflection point if positive.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. General Fusion Group Ltd. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. title: REG - Intl Con Airline Grp - Launch of €500 million share buyback programme - TradingView
content: Further to IAG’s announcement on 26 February 2026 of a €1,500 million return of excess cash to shareholders, and following completion of the second €500 million share buyback programme after the final purchase on 10 September 2026, IAG announces the launch of a final €500 million share buyback programme (the “Programme”), completing the €1,500 million return of excess cash announced in February 2026. Shares acquired under the Programme are expected to be cancelled pursuant to the capital reduction approved at the Company’s Shareholders’ Meeting held on 18 June 2026. The Programme will be carried out pursuant to the authorisation granted by the Annual General Meeting held on 18 June 2026. Morgan Stanley Europe SE (“MS”) and Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE ("GS") have been engaged to implement the Programme in sequential portions. MS and GS (and/or their respective delegates) will make the share purchases on the Company's behalf (acting as riskless principal and not as agent) and make all trading decisions independently of, and uninfluenced by, the Company, subject to certain parameters agreed between the Company and each of MS and GS prior to the commencement of the Programme. Qatar Airways Group Q.C.S.C. (“Qatar Airways”) has agreed to participate in the Programme on a pro rata basis in order to preserve its aggregate stake in IAG at the level held immediately prior to the implementation of the Company’s recent share buyback programmes, the first of which was announced on 8 November 2024 (i.e. 25.1434% of IAG’s voting rights). Under the arrangements entered into with MS and GS, Qatar Airways has agreed not to sell IAG shares in the market during the Programme. Instead, it will sell to MS and GS, as applicable, for on-sale to the Company, on each trading day a number of shares proportionate to the number of shares bought by such bank in the market on that day, at a price per share equal to the volume weighted average price at which such bank purchased such shares in the market on that day. The Programme will be executed through purchases of shares from market participants and purchases of shares from Qatar Airways on the terms set out above, in an aggregate amount of up to €500 million (€374 million for purchases from market participants and €126 million for purchases from Qatar Airways). The Programme will start on 5 October 2026 and is expected to end no later than 26 February 2027, unless terminated by the Company, MS or GS, as applicable, in certain circumstances. The Programme will be carried out in accordance with the provisions of the Market Abuse Regulation (EU) 596/2014 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1052 (including as incorporated into UK law) regarding the exemption for buyback programmes, and will have the following characteristics: a)    Regulated market: the shares will be purchased on both the London Stock Exchange and the Spanish Stock Exchanges (each an "Exchange"). b)    Maximum pecuniary amount allocated to the Programme: €500,000,000, with up to €374,283,000 allocated to purchases of shares from market participants. c)    Maximum number of shares to be acquired pursuant to the Programme: up to 210,000,000 ordinary shares, representing approximately 4.55 per cent. of the Company's issued share capital as of 2 October 2026. d)    Consideration per share: the shares will be purchased at a price of no more than the lower of: (i) the higher of the price of the last independent trade and the highest then current independent purchase bid on the Exchange where the purchase is carried out, and (ii) 105 per cent. of the average market value of the shares for the five business days prior to the day the purchase is made. e)    Maximum volume per trading session (including share purchases from both market participants and from Qatar Airways): no more than 25 per cent. of the average daily volume of the shares traded on the Exchange in the 20 trading days immediately preceding the date of purchase. Shares acquired pursuant to the Programme will be held in treasury, pending their proposed cancellation, which was approved IAG’s Annual General Meeting on 18 June 2026. title: BMW R 1250 GS (2019-2023) - Review & Buying Guide - Bennetts Insurance
content: In 2019 BMW didn’t need to reinvent the wheel. In fact, they didn’t even really need to fix a small puncture in its tyre. The R1200GS was fairly comfortably still the adventure bike to beat and while rivals such as the Triumph Tiger 1200, Honda Africa Twin or Ducati Multistrada 1260 were doing their best to take a slice of its pie, buyers were still picking the GS over them in far greater numbers and few were in danger of changing brands if they already owned a BMW. But, not a company to rest on its laurels (mainly as the GS represented such a huge percentage of their annual sales...), in 2019 BMW decided to give the GS a bit of a performance upgrade. A fairly minor update in many ways, the R1200GS evolved into the R1250GS and with it gained a bit more capacity and a ShiftCam element within the motor. Naturally there were refinements to its many electronic assists but realistically, this upgrade was all about giving the boxer motor a bit more performance without ruining the overall balance of the GS. Did BMW succeed in this quest? Oh yes, the R1250GS is undeniably the best of the ‘old-school’ GS models before the R1300GS arrived and made everything more compact and sportier - which it has to be said isn’t to everyone’s tastes... Recommended retail price is rather a distracting point with a GS because there is no real set price due to the number of options, paint schemes and variations available. Back in 2019 in the UK there was the option of a stock GS (£13,415) or the TE (£16,500), which had more bells and whistles. And that’s before you add in Option 719 or HP accessories into the equation! Did we mention paint? Yep, there were two basic paint options (Blackstorm and Cosmic Blue) but the Exclusive model added blacked-out details while the HP was more off-road influenced and had a Light White/Racing Blue paint scheme and spoke wheels. Got that? Ok. Nowadays you really need to be looking for a TE model (the majority sold are TEs) as that has more options fitted. Prices start at £7999 for a high-mileage example but you can get a good one for in the region of £8999 that has less than 20,000 miles on its clocks, which is a better idea. A fair few come with luggage, which is always good to see. The HP generally commands a few quid extra as it does look cool and riders like its spoke wheels. Although the GS was updated in 2020 (to celebrate its 40th anniversary), this basically just involved ABS Pro, DTC and an Eco riding mode becoming standard fitment with full-LED lights an optional extra but as the majority of bikes sold are TEs with angle-responsive assists upgrade this isn’t a huge concern to used buyers. And neither is the pretty horrible 40th Anniversary black/yellow paint option, which is best avoided unless you really like it... So what exactly has changed within the boxer motor? Quite a lot actually. The R1200GS had a capacity of 1170cc, which has been expanded to 1254cc through both a bigger bore (102.5mm from 101mm) and stroke (76mm from 73mm) on the R1250GS and this obviously necessitated new pistons. According to BMW, the capacity increase saw the GS gain 7% more power (up from 125bhp to 136bhp) and also 14% more torque (up from 125Nm to 143Nm). And alongside this growth a new ShiftCam system arrived... Activated on the intake side only, BMW say ShiftCam helps enhance torque and improve fuel economy while also optimising emissions to allow the GS to hit stricter limits as well as future targets. Other changes include a vertical flow cylinder head, the use of a toothed cam chain, a revised gearbox and much more. However, despite all these updates, the great thing about the R1250GS is that it feels just like an R1200GS – just better! Hop on the GS and you instantly spot that wonderfully raw and meaty drive that owners love, yet in this new evolution it punches even harder just where you want it to. Driving with a beautiful amount of flexibility, it’s a great motor and one that is also remarkably brisk when you want it to be. Yet should you decide to take it easy, it’s just as happy burbling around at low revs. There really is very little to criticise (aside from Dynamic mode possibly being a touch too spirited) and even the quickshifter is smooth and predictable in its action. With GS models only six years old at most, there isn’t really that much to concern yourself about when it comes to the engine’s reliability. Yes, a full service history from an authorised BMW dealership is recommended, but there are lots of GSs that have covered over 30,000 miles in their fairly short lifespan so if you buy one with just 10,000 miles on its clocks you can expect it to keep on going for many more care-free miles. That said, it has been subject to three recalls (two in 2020, one in 2023) – although one was for an incorrectly bonded sticker! Not all bikes are affected, so check you VIN. As so many GS models were sold there are various internet stories about issues such as a ticking from the motor (lefthand side, apparently there is an updated tensioner), leaks, sensors failing and dodgy batteries but generally, they are extremely reliable. It’s unlikely you will buy a lemon, especially if it has a full BMW service history. And should you buy from a BMW dealer, you should be able to get  an extended warranty (two years) – although T&Cs apply. The R1250GS and R1200GS’s chassis (ok, bolt-on subframes...) are pretty much identical however the R1250GS has the next evolution of Dynamic ESA. Called ‘Next Generation’, it comes with fully-automatic load compensation as well as the option of an off-road optimised system (only on the HP model). A slightly enhanced system when compared to the old Dynamic ESA, it does make the GS ride smoother and more level but as it has a Telelever, most riders won’t really notice the upgrade unless they are changing from the old R1200GS model. As with all ESA system, check all the functions are working and that there are no signs of leaks from the shocks as they are expensive to replace with BMW units and often not 100% reliable if rebuilt by aftermarket firms. On higher-mileage bikes feel for any slight weave at low speed that hints at the Telelever requiring new ball joints and also check the rear hub for leaks or any bearing grumbles – generally both last well over 40,000 miles without needing servicing. Some owners swear by removing the drive shaft and greasing the splines but this is a job best left to a professional unless you are very confident, stick with replacing the oil every 6000 miles as it’s much easier to do! When it comes to brakes, the GSs units come in for some online criticism. Unlike the old model that came with Brembo brakes, the R1250GS has BMW branded items made by American firm Hayes. A few owners have experienced issues and it is odd that GS Adventure models arrived with Brembo units, not the BMW-branded items – although not all. According to VOSA there wasn’t an official recall but a fair few owners seem to have been back to their dealer to get the calipers looked at. The GS is a superb mile-muncher and although the Adventure has not only a bigger tank but also enhanced weather protection, it can be a touch intimidating at low speeds, especially for shorter riders. You can generally expect anything from 45mpg to 55mpg from a GS, giving it a tank range of 200-250 miles. Due to the relaxed riding position and extensive creature comforts (BMW’s heated grip are excellent), you can keep on motoring on a GS and only the fuel warning light will stop your progress. Oddly, a taller screen generally isn’t a huge benefit (especially for taller riders) and you are better off using a small screen as the windblast helps support your body where a tall screen can create a lot of helmet buffeting (unless you add a deflector). Where do we start? Ok, the stock GS has two riding modes (Road and Rain) alongside Automatic Stability Control (ASC, BMW’s non-angle-responsive traction control system), ABS and Hill Start Control. Riding Modes Pro adds Dynamic, Dynamic Pro, Enduro and Enduro Pro riding modes. Dynamic Traction Control (DTC) is BMW’s cornering traction control, which is usually fitted alongside ABS Pro, BMW’s cornering ABS system (both standard fitment from 2020). Hill Start Control Pro and Dynamic Brake Assistant (DBC) are optional extras and so is Dynamic ESA, Intelligent Emergency Call and Shift Assistant Pro. Phew! Generally speaking, a TE model has DTC, Dynamic ESA, ABS Pro, Shift Assistant Pro and Riding Modes Pro but always check just to be sure. When it comes to accessories, luggage is always popular and most riders either go for BMW’s panniers and top box or Touratech’s versions. Tall screens are also quite common and so are practical add-ons such as crash bars, mudguard extenders, fog lights etc. The GS is quite price-sensitive to accessories and the level of spec, mainly as there are so many out there for sale good ones (or ones with a high spec) tend to stand out. When buying used, just check the dash hasn’t got any signs of misting, a few were leaky, or glitches and faults... Generally, buyers of a GS want a GS. However there are some excellent rivals out there that shouldn’t be overlooked. The BMW R1250GS is undisputedly the best of the old-school GS models and many would argue it feels more of a ‘GS’ than the current R1300GS. Big, robust and able to turn its hand to any task, this is a fabulous bike that sat at the top of the adventure bike tree for its entire lifespan. If you have ever questioned why the GS is such an institution and BMW’s best-selling model by a mile, take an R1250GS out for a test ride – you may very well end up riding home on it! title: GS Retail holds cemetery cleanup at Seoul National Cemetery on Armed Forces Day - 헤럴드경제
content: GS Retail held a cemetery cleanup at Seoul National Cemetery in Dongjak-gu, Seoul, on Thursday — Armed Forces Day — with CEO Heo Seo-hong and 53 executives taking part. The activity was organized to honor fallen soldiers who sacrificed their lives for the country and to help bereaved families and visitors pay their respects in a well-maintained environment. The executives paid their respects at the Memorial Tower and signed the guest book before moving to Section 39, which holds more than 1,100 graves of Korean War soldiers — including those who died in the Battle of Hill 1090 — where they cleaned headstones and removed weeds. GS Retail has conducted volunteer activities at Seoul National Cemetery, with participation from its CEO and employees, since 2019. Since 2024, the company has formalized the partnership through a sister-organization agreement with the cemetery, committing to two cleanup sessions per year focused on Section 39. Last year, the company extended its volunteer efforts to the National Daejeon Cemetery. This year, about 25 employees from the Daejeon area took part in a cleanup there on May 29, collecting litter and tidying the grounds. "We will continue to carry out ESG activities that reflect the spirit of honoring national service and put patriotic values into practice," said Park Gyeong-rang, head of GS Retail's ESG division.

title: Global Institute Dialogues: Jason Bordoff on the Geopolitics of Energy - Goldman Sachs
content:
We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Jason Bordoff is the Founding Director, Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. In this edition of Global Institute Dialogues, Jason Bordoff discusses how the Iran crisis, China’s electrification strategy, and the US shale revolution have changed energy geopolitics. The views stated herein are those of the interviewee and do not necessarily reflect the views of Goldman Sachs or its affiliates. Goldman Sachs is not responsible for any statements made by the interviewee. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been called the worst oil shock in history. During the Iran conflict, however, oil futures have not yet surpassed their 2008 peak. What does that tell us about the risks that Hormuz poses to the global economy, as well as the sources of market resilience? It is too early to say with certainty what the full oil market effects will be, since the crisis is far from over. But a few things are already clear. Closing the Strait of Hormuz— through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and LNG supplies flowed before the crisis—has long been the nightmare scenario of energy security planning; the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA) called it the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. Yet with the strait almost entirely closed for nearly four months, Brent averaged just over $100 a barrel, up from around $70 when the war began, and peaked at $126 in April—far below the $200 that veteran analysts had warned was possible. Several factors explain the muted response, and most were neither automatic nor guaranteed. Markets were oversupplied and inventories relatively flush when the war began. Saudi and Emirati pipelines, built years ago as insurance, moved over five million additional barrels a day around the strait, cutting the shortfall in Gulf exports to roughly 13 million barrels a day rather than the full 20 million. The IEA coordinated the largest emergency stock release in its history, which, together with commercial draws, offset five million to six million barrels a day. US production and exports surged, and refiners proved remarkably flexible in responding to price signals. Perhaps the biggest surprise was China, which cut imports by roughly five million barrels a day between February and June by halting strategic purchases, drawing down inventories, restricting refined product exports, and reducing domestic demand. The lesson is not that Hormuz no longer matters. It is that resilience was purchased—through years of investment— and that those buffers are now considerably more threadbare and should not be taken for granted. Major energy crises often lead to structural shifts in energy markets. What lasting transformations do you expect the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to create in the global energy landscape? Lasting transformations in the global energy system are hard to predict with confidence. But the energy world had already changed dramatically before this shock: The United States is now the world’s largest oil and gas producer; renewables and electric vehicles have become genuine alternatives in some sectors; a cooperative global order has given way to geopolitical fragmentation; and China, India, and other emerging economies now drive demand growth. The most consequential shift this crisis has revealed is a new geography of energy power. The countries best able to absorb disruption and those forced to bear its costs are no longer the same. The United States weathered this shock far better than it would have a decade ago, given both lower oil use as a share of GDP and much higher production. China, as the largest importer and by far the largest holder of inventories, has come to play an important balancing role in the global market. Meanwhile, the burden of demand adjustment has shifted toward poorer importing countries with thinner fiscal buffers: Jet fuel spot prices briefly approached $200 a barrel in some markets, and dozens of developing economies adopted nearly 200 emergency measures, from rationing and conservation mandates to fuel tax suspensions. Expect a durable turn toward redundancy as countries invest to make the oil and gas system more resilient, not just to move away from it. Infrastructure once considered surplus, such as Saudi Arabia’s East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, proved vital; both Saudi Arabia and the UAE plan to increase their bypass capacity; and Iraq and Kuwait are exploring new export routes. Governments are rebuilding or expanding buffers; the United States should appropriate funds to refill and modernize a strategic petroleum reserve (SPR), now at its lowest level in nearly five decades, while India, South Africa, and Southeast Asian countries are seeking to build reserves and refining capacity. Electrification will accelerate too, but not automatically, and not necessarily in a low-carbon direction without policy direction. China has undergone one of the largest electrification and clean-energy build-outs in history. How is China’s energy strategy evolving, and what does it mean for global energy markets and strategic competition? For more than two decades, China has pursued an energy security strategy built for precisely this kind of disruption. At the core of this strategy is electrification: Shifting the economy away from directly consuming oil and gas reduces exposure to markets prone to geopolitical shocks. The transformation has been historic. More than 32 percent of China’s final energy consumption is now electricity, against 22 percent in the United States and 21 percent in Europe. More than half of new cars sold are electric. China invested $625 billion in clean energy in 2024, nearly one-third of the global total, and clean-energy sectors contributed over 10 percent of GDP in 2025. The Hormuz crisis showed the benefits of that strategy. It was part of the reason China reduced oil imports by roughly five million barrels a day, easing pressure on global markets; China also restricted refined product exports (imposing significant costs on its Asian neighbors), drew inventories, and ceased filling its stocks. If the crisis continues and worsens, with OECD inventories depleted, China’s estimated 1.4 billion barrels of strategic reserves, drawn down only modestly so far, are now among the last lines of defense against a sharper price spike. For decades, US presidents called Riyadh during oil crises to ask for spare capacity; Beijing may come to occupy a comparable position, with comparable influence. The 15th Five-Year Plan calls for China to become an “energy powerhouse,” and Beijing recently raised its 2030 renewable consumption target by 53 percent—which will mean both more renewables and more coal. Paired with China’s dominance of clean energy supply chains—over 80 percent of solar, wind, and battery manufacturing capacity, plus most critical minerals processing—this leaves other countries choosing not whether to depend on imports but which dependence is least dangerous. China’s behavior in this crisis to look out for itself by moving quickly to restrict refined products exports, viewed by some as prioritizing domestic energy security at the expense of neighboring Asian countries, may make that trade-off look less attractive. The shale revolution made the United States the world’s top oil and gas producer. To what extent has that changed the United States’ geopolitical position, and what does the country need to do to maintain it? Combined with lower oil intensity, the shale revolution has fundamentally strengthened America’s geopolitical position, and this crisis demonstrated it. The US economy is nearly four times larger than in 1973, while domestic oil demand is only slightly higher. Two decades ago, the country imported 60 percent of the oil it used; this spring, it became the world’s largest oil exporter and briefly a net crude exporter for the first time since World War II. Oil is globally priced, so Americans still feel higher pump prices. But the broader damage has been far smaller than it once was: Economists at the Dallas Fed estimate a shock comparable to this year’s would have cut US real GDP growth by 5.6 percentage points in 1980, versus roughly 0.3 points today. As a net exporter, the United States saw higher prices transfer income to domestic producers, workers, and shareholders rather than abroad. In an acute disruption, physical barrels can price far above futures benchmarks, forcing import-dependent economies in Europe and Asia to pay steep premiums for immediate delivery; abundant domestic production gave the United States a valuable window of insulation from these dislocations. The contrast was even starker in natural gas, where European and Asian prices moved toward $20 per million BTUs while US benchmarks stayed below $3 per million BTUs—an example of a divergence the economist Lucas Davis estimates has saved American consumers roughly $5 trillion over two decades. Maintaining this position means resisting the temptation to squander it: Refill and modernize the SPR; keep export markets open rather than yielding to calls for restrictions that could damage US credibility and undermine domestic production and refining capacity; and preserve the efficiency, mass transit, and EV policies that reduce oil exposure. America’s newfound position as a dominant producer also means recognizing an uncomfortable corollary—a superpower insulated from the consequences of the turmoil in which it’s involved has fewer reasons for restraint. For investors, what are the most important trends in the energy transition? Where is the market overestimating change, and where is it underestimating it? The most important trend for investors is that the energy transition is no longer driven by climate policy alone. Energy security, industrial strategy, and national security have become equally important and increasingly inseparable. Markets may be overestimating the speed and linearity of the move away from fossil fuels. Every oil and gas shock strengthens the case for electrification, but wanting secure and affordable energy does not necessarily mean moving quickly off all fossil fuels. This crisis, for example, pushed several Asian countries toward coal—Japan allowed greater use of older plants, South Korea lifted limits on coal-fired generation, and India accelerated a $4 billion coal-to-chemicals plan—and the IEA expects record global coal consumption this year. Some governments may also conclude that if the nightmare scenario proved manageable, the practical course is to invest in the resilience of the oil and gas system rather than to move beyond it. Investors should understand both today’s headwinds and its tailwinds for the energy transition. On one hand, clean energy is more capital-intensive, which is especially challenging in an era of higher interest rates. Moreover, in a world of geopolitical fragmentation, governments are shifting from “just in time” to “just in case”: storage, redundant pipelines and ports, strategic reserves, domestic refining, and trusted supply chains. The desire to de-risk from global supply chains dominated by China will lead many governments to feel a growing pull toward energy autarky—the ability to meet one’s own energy needs. The problem is that prioritizing redundancy and domestic manufacturing and extraction is inflationary for clean energy. On the other hand, the drive to reduce exposure to geopolitically risky oil and gas markets will lead many governments to try to reduce imports, giving a push to electrification and domestic sources of electricity, including clean-energy technologies such as solar, wind, geothermal, storage, and nuclear. Electrification, such as EVs and heat pumps, and clean sources of electricity are themselves tools of geopolitical resilience; indeed, energy security, which has returned to the forefront as a policy concern, can be a more powerful driver of clean energy than climate change alone. About the Interviewee
Jason Bordoff is Founding Director of the Center on Global Energy Policy, and Professor of Professional Practice in International and Public Relations at Columbia University SIPA. Bordoff is also Cofounding Dean Emeritus of the Columbia Climate School. Bordoff joined the Columbia University faculty after serving until January 2013 as Special Assistant to President Barack Obama and Senior Director for Energy and Climate Change on the staff of the National Security Council, and, prior to that, holding senior policy positions on the White House’s National Economic Council and Council on Environmental Quality. One of the world’s leading energy and climate policy experts, Bordoff places research and policy interests at the intersection of economics, energy, environment, and national security. He has written prolifically about how to address our greatest energy and climate change challenges and has developed innovative programs and tools to train future leaders to bridge the gap between academic research and policy, focused on delivering research insights in formats and time frames that are accessible and useful to decision-makers outside of academia. title: 2027 BMW F 450 R First Look - Motorcycle.com
content: BMW announced a new lightweight naked bike based on the F 450 GS adventure bike for 2027. The new F 450 R replaces the G 310 R as the smallest naked model in BMW’s lineup, and a potential stepping stone to the larger bikes. The F 450 R shares the GS model’s 420cc parallel-Twin engine, but uses a stainless steel underslung muffler and a more road-focused tuning. Developed with the help of TVS Motor, the engine produces a claimed peak output of 47 hp at 8,750 rpm, or the maximum amount to meet European A2 licensing requirements. BMW also claims a maximum of 31.8 lb-ft. of torque at 6,750 rpm, with 80% of it available at 3,000 rpm. According to BMW, the F 450 R can get 61.9 mpg. Combined with a 3.7-gallon fuel tank, that works out to a range of about 229 miles on a full tank. The engine is matched with a six-speed transmission, which can be reversed to a 1-up, 5-down shift pattern for track use. All but the base level trim come equipped with BMW’s Shift Assistant Pro bidirectional quickshifter, while the top-tier M Sport with Innovation Package trim adds a centrifugal Easy Ride Clutch for pulling away or coming to a stop without needing to touch the clutch lever. The F 450 R uses a ride-by-wire throttle with three selectable ride modes: Rain, Road, and Dynamic. Other standard electronic systems include the lean-sensitive ABS Pro, Dynamic Brake Control for preventing unintended throttle use during braking, Dynamic Traction Control, and engine drag torque control (MSR). The steel trellis frame is based on the F 450 GS’ chassis, but with a few adjustments for road use including a shorter wheelbase (55.3 inches for the F 450 R versus 57.7 inches for the GS). Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window. KYB provides the suspension system. Up front, the base model F 450 R uses a 43mm inverted fork, with the higher trims adding adjustable rebound and compression damping. The fork is paired with a monoshock connected directly to the double-sided swingarm, offering adjustable preload and rebound damping. Suspension travel is 5.5 inches on either end. The front wheel is equipped with a single radial-mount Brembo four-piston monoblock caliper and a 310mm disc. A single-piston ByBre floating caliper and 240mm disc are used for the rear. Other standard features include full LED lighting, a 6.5-inch TFT display, smartphone connectivity, a USB-C port, heated grips, and forged aluminum foot controls and kickstand. BMW claims a curb weight of 386 pounds (388 pounds with the Easy Ride Clutch). The 2027 BMW F 450 R will come in four trim variants. The base model is only available in Cosmic Black. The Exclusive Trim also comes in black, but adds Shift Assistant Pro and an adjustable fork. The next step up is the F 450 R M Sport, which comes in Snaefell white / M Motorsport with a white frame and rim stickers. It also adds a Dynamic Pro ride mode on top of the quickshifter and adjustable fork. The Innovation Package adds the Easy Ride Clutch to the M Sport trim. As of this writing, BMW has not confirmed U.S. availability, but we expect a formal announcement to come in due time. title: Bruno Mars Asks Karol G to ‘Dance With Me’ in New Music Video - billboard.com
content:
The singer found a way to "get her back" after Drake stole the spotlight with Karol at her Houston concert. Bruno Mars may have just found the perfect way to get Karol G back. Just days after joking that he needed to “get” the Colombian superstar back from Drake, Mars has recruited Karol G for the new music video for his lovely The Romantic track “Dance With Me,” released Thursday (Oct. 1). The video opens with Mars strumming an electric guitar all by his lonesome, pleading the lyrics into a pay phone. Karol is on the other line, sulking in bed in a lace outfit. Mars moves on from the telephone booth to where Karol resides, serenading her from below her balcony with a full band behind him. It’s a dreamy, old-fashioned serenade, with Mars singing to Karol as the instruments flourish. Karol makes her way below, jumping into Mars’ arms as fireworks explode in the sky. The duo stares into each other’s eyes as the video comes to a close, ending the night on a wholesome — and, quite literally, a romantic — note. It’s a fitting visual for “Dance With Me,” which finds Mars leaning into the kind of swooning romance that has become a signature theme within his discography. And Karol G’s appearance comes at a bit of a funny time in their ongoing musical friendship. On Monday (Sept. 28), Mars reacted to a viral video of Drake dancing with Karol G during the rapper’s surprise appearance at her Houston concert. Posting a photo of himself staring dramatically out of the window of a private jet, Mars jokingly wrote, “I have to get her back! I must get her back! I will get her back!” Mars and Karol G already have some musical history together, as the pair teamed up on “Still,” an all-English-synth-pop ballad from Karol G’s sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto. The collaboration reached No. 41 on the Billboard Hot 100, while the album debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200. They also took “Still” to the stage together for the first time when Mars surprised fans during Karol G’s Aug. 15 concert at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium. For Mars, “Dance With Me” is the closing track on The Romantic, his first solo album in nearly a decade. title: GS Entec wins contract for 37 monopiles at Taean OWF - Ocean Energy Resources
content: GLOBAL NEWS SERVICE FOR THE FOSSIL AND RENEWABLE ENERGY COMMUNITIES GS Entec has signed a contract to supply 37 monopiles for a 504MW offshore wind farm off the coast of Taean, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea. Production is scheduled to begin in July 2027, with delivery to be completed by the end of August 2028. The contract value was not disclosed. The order comes immediately after the company invested approximately 300 billion won (approximately $221.5 million) to expand its annual production capacity from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons, a more than threefold increase.   The dynamic brake light effectively alerts following vehicles that the

According to Woofun AI, Goldman Sachs (GS.US), based on August personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data and the latest remarks by New York Fed President John Williams, has officially pushed back its expectation for the Federal Reserve's second rate hike this year from October to December, while noting that the likelihood of ultimately needing no further rate hikes has increased significantly. This revision in the forecast marks a significant shift on Wall Street regarding the trajectory of monetary policy. The underlying rationale is that recent inflation indicators have failed to sustain their earlier improvement, while market‑based measures have remained steady around 3% both before and after the statistical methodology change—still well above the Fed's 2% target. "The New Fed News Agency" columnist Nick Timiraos notes that despite strong readings in June and July, August's data showed no continuation of the disinflationary trend. Coupled with earlier weak PPI and CPI figures, the market had already anticipated this development; thus, the PCE data did not deliver any game‑changing insights but rather confirmed the reality that inflation has been stuck at elevated levels since April 2025, failing to make progress toward the 2% target. Goldman Sachs' economics team, led by Jan Hatzius, explicitly noted in its report that the core PCE price index rose 0.25% month-over-month and 3.01% year-over-year—well below market expectations. This prompted them to lower their forecast for fourth-quarter core PCE year-over-year growth to 3%, a figure significantly below the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) participants' median projection of 3.4%, thereby reinforcing the view that rate hikes will be paused in October and action may not resume until December. At the analyst level, differing institutions exhibit significant divergence in their interpretations of inflationary pressures, reflecting market uncertainty over the timing of a policy pivot. Stephen Brown, Chief North American Economist at Capital Economics, adopts a relatively dovish stance, arguing that core price pressures are slightly less severe than previously feared and supporting the view that the Fed will pause rate hikes in October. He specifically notes that the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)'s recent revision to the PCE methodology has led to downward revisions in historical core inflation data, with these adjustments collectively reducing core inflation by roughly 0.3 percentage points. Coupled with the downward revisions for June and July, this brings the annualized pace of core inflation over the past three months down to 2%, providing statistical support for a pause in rate increases. However, Sal Guatieri, a senior economist at BMO (BMO.US), offered a more cautious assessment, arguing that the underlying trend in inflation has not shown any substantial improvement. According to data compiled by Woofun AI, although the share of PCE price components with annualized increases exceeding 3% has declined from 54% to 51%, it remains well above normal levels—hardly enough to suggest that the fundamental inflationary trend has been fundamentally reversed. Guatieri emphasized that this structural pressure will reinforce the Federal Reserve's view that further policy tightening is still needed to bring inflation back to its target, thereby offsetting some of the easing expectations stemming from the recent cooling of short-term data. This divergence highlights the complexity of current inflation data: on the one hand, the deceleration in month-over-month growth provides some breathing room; on the other hand, the year-on-year base effect and persistent structural components of high inflation continue to pose a dilemma for policymakers. Market pricing has swiftly captured this subtle shift in policy expectations, yet volatility remains pronounced. According to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool, the market currently assigns roughly a 39% probability to a rate hike in October, down from about 45% prior to the release of the PCE data, indicating that investors have scaled back their bets on the near-term pace of monetary tightening. Meanwhile, the probability of a rate hike in December has surged to 90%, signaling that the market has clearly pushed back the window for tightening. In the bond market, the yield on the 2-year U.S. Treasury note fell sharply from 4.887% to around 4.864% following the release of the PCE data, directly reflecting investors' waning expectations regarding the urgency of near-term Fed rate hikes. However, this downward trend did not persist; yields subsequently rebounded, fully reversing their earlier decline, underscoring that market concerns about persistent long-term inflation remain. Meanwhile, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield continued to rise, further confirming that long-term interest rates are driven by both economic resilience and inflation expectations. This dynamic shift in the yield curve suggests that, despite a decline in the probability of near-term rate hikes, the market has not yet pivoted fully to an easing bias. Instead, it has repriced both the terminal level and the pace of the hiking cycle, underscoring continued respect for the Fed's "higher for longer" policy stance. The robust resilience of macroeconomic fundamentals provides a solid underpinning for inflationary stickiness, making it difficult for the Federal Reserve to pivot easily toward easing. U.S. second-quarter GDP growth was sharply revised up to an annualized 2.2%, well above the previously reported 1.5%, signaling economic momentum that far exceeded expectations. Both consumption and investment—two key components—outperformed their prior readings; in particular, the critical measure of endogenous growth momentum—real private domestic final sales—was also revised upward to 4.6%, underscoring strong domestic demand. The upward revision in investment largely reflects the boost to growth from AI‑related infrastructure spending, while the higher estimate for consumer spending indicates that, supported by a resilient labor market and a buoyant stock market, households' financial conditions remain broadly sound. In August, consumer spending rose 0.9% month over month, partly driven by higher gasoline expenditures amid rising oil prices, while income growth edged down slightly from 0.3% last month to 0.2%. Meanwhile, the overall PCE price index increased 3.4% year over year, unchanged from the previous month, with month‑over‑month growth accelerating to 0.3%. This set of data indicates that, although the deceleration in the month-over-month growth of the PCE has reduced the urgency of a rate hike in October, robust economic expansion and resilient consumer spending suggest that inflationary pressures will not ease quickly. Consequently, the Federal Reserve must remain cautious in balancing growth and inflation, as any premature easing could heighten the risk of an inflationary rebound. title: 2027 Federal Pay Freeze: How Are 2027 GS Pay Scales with Locality Calculated? - fedagent.com
content: The end of the calendar year often brings updates to General Schedule (GS) Pay Scales for the Federal workforce.  Here’s an in-depth look at the essential details for 2027 to help you navigate your compensation and make informed decisions for your financial future. On August 26, 2026, President Trump officially submitted an alternative pay plan. This proposal includes a pay freeze on both base and locality pay for most Civilian Federal Employees. The proposal cited fiscal responsibility and economic conditions. The planned pay freeze does make an exception for Federal law enforcement, proposing a 3.8% raise starting in January, as well as service members, with a 5-7% raise for active military and 3.6% pay increase for other uniformed service members. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) will determine which law enforcement positions are eligible for the 3.8% raise next year. Federal employees received a 1% base pay raise in 2026, after an initial proposed pay raise, but no locality pay raise. The proposed pay freeze would also leave locality pay unchanged from 2026. There are currently 53 locality pay areas. The United States Office of Personnel Management (OPM) uses three factors to calculate GS pay scales. This system applies to most Civilian Feds under the General Schedule, excluding those covered by Executive and Senior Level Pay Tables. The GS Pay Grade system includes 15 categories of pay ranges. GS-1 is the lowest, and GS-15 is the highest. Jobs are assigned a grade based on the level of responsibility, qualifications, and experience. For example, a position that requires a high school diploma but no experience in that field may be a GS-2 position. A position that requires a master’s degree is usually a GS-9. The GS Pay Step system divides each pay grade into 10 steps. Each step is worth about 3% of the employee’s salary, so the higher the step, the higher the salary. Promotions and seniority-based milestones lead to higher steps. In general, it takes 18 years to move from the lowest to the highest step within a single grade. Locality relates to the region where the employee works. This factor adjusts the base rate of pay for the cost of living in a geographic area. While each position is assigned to a specific grade, and each employee is assigned to a step within that grade, the pay rate will vary by location. This ensures fair compensation in high-cost areas like California or major metropolitan areas. While the system may seem complicated, these three factors help address the most fundamental questions involved in compensating a workforce: ·       The differences between positions in terms of responsibilities, difficulties, requirements, etc. ·       The need to compensate long-term workers for their service. ·       The cost-of-living differences when the workforce is located all over the country. Of the three determining factors, locality adjustments can be the most complicated to predict. The amount of the adjustment is calculated as a percentage rate based on data from the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics Annual National Compensation Survey. This tool gathers data on compensation from government and non-government sectors in locations all over the country. This information is then compared to the base pay of federal employees in similar positions to calculate the locality pay adjustment factor. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) defines 53 locality areas that OPM uses in setting locality adjustments for all 50 states and all United States territories and possessions. OMB uses defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas and Combined Statistical Areas for this purpose. Hawaii and Alaska have their own pay scales, and 51 other locality areas center on major metropolitan areas. Locations inside the continental United States that don’t fall into an established locality area are grouped as “Rest of United States.” Year over year, OPM recommends changes as needed. The President recommends wholesale adjustments to the pay scales, and they are then approved by Congress each year. Federal employees working abroad are not eligible for locality pay adjustments. How Can I Use the Locality Pay Adjustment Factor Information? Civilian Feds often earn more because of the locality pay adjustment factor. You can find the adjustment rate for your locality by visiting the locality area pay definitions published by OPM. This tool is also useful if you’re considering applying for a similar position in a different part of the country; you can estimate how much higher or lower the pay might be in a new location. One of the most important reasons to thoroughly understand your current and future compensation is to calculate your family’s insurance and benefits needs. title: GS Entec to supply 37 monopiles for Taean offshore wind farm - Korea JoongAng Daily
content: The contract comes as GS Entec works to expands its production capacity to capture growing demand for large-scale offshore wind projects. GS Entec, a major plant equipment manufacturer and subsidiary of GS Global, will supply 37 monopiles to a planned offshore wind farm off Taean, South Chungcheong, as it expands its production capacity to capture growing demand for large-scale offshore wind projects, the company said on Wednesday. Under the contract signed with Taean Wind Power, a joint venture company developing a major 504-megawatt offshore wind farm off the coast of Taean, GS Entec will start production in July 2027 and finish deliveries by the end of August 2028. Monopiles are large steel tubes driven into the seabed to support wind turbines and their towers. According to GS Entec, more than 70 percent of offshore wind projects worldwide use them. The 504-megawatt wind farm is jointly developed by Singapore-based Vena Energy, Danish investor Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Korea Western Power. Construction is set to begin in 2028, and completion is targeted for 2030. Once running, the farm is expected to generate enough electricity for about 300,000 households a year. GS Entec supplied all 64 monopiles for the Yeonggwang Nakwol offshore wind project in 2023. This month, it completed a 300 billion won ($220.8 million) plant expansion. The expansion raised its annual production capacity from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons. “Based on our accumulated technology and expanded production capacity, we will win more orders in the domestic and overseas offshore wind substructure markets and keep pace with the government’s push to expand offshore wind power,” a GS Entec representative said. The U.S. president said Korea could face unspecified additional charges if it does not join the Alaska liquefied natural gas project. Nearly 3 million foreign visitors came to Busan through July, fueling sharp gains for department stores, beauty retailers and local businesses. The sale, equivalent to 2.3 percent of the group’s holding company, will occur in blocks to avoid dis-rupting the market. The Korean titan is set to post an earnings call high despite analyst apprehension over a strengthening won, and the market shows little sign of slowing down.

Business GS Entec to supply 37 monopiles for Taean wind project GS Entec, a subsidiary of GS Global, will supply 37 monopiles for the 504-megawatt Taean offshore wind farm off the coast of Taean, South Chungcheong Province. Under a contract signed Wednesday at the Seoul headquarters of Taean Wind Power, GS Entec will begin production in July 2027 and complete deliveries by the end of August 2028. Monopiles are cylindrical steel foundations that support offshore wind turbines and towers. They can be used in waters up to about 50 meters deep and are generally more cost- and time-efficient than jacket foundations that use a lattice framework. The shallow waters and thick sedimentary layers off Taean make the area suitable for monopile foundations. The Taean offshore wind project is being jointly developed by Singapore-based renewable energy developer Vena Energy, Danish infrastructure investor Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Korea Western Power. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028 and finish in 2030. Once completed, the farm is expected to power about 300,000 households for a year. The company entered the monopile business in 2022 through a strategic technology partnership with Dutch company Sif. It supplied all 64 monopiles for the Yeonggwang Nakwol offshore wind project in 2023 and has since secured the Taean project. The company is one of the few in South Korea with experience mass-producing and delivering large monopiles from a single domestic plant. GS Entec also completed a plant expansion after investing about 300 billion won ($220 million). The expansion increased annual production capacity from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons, with the Taean project set to utilize the expanded capacity. The manufacturer is also being considered as a foundation supplier for the 340-megawatt Hanbit project, following the implementation of the Offshore Wind Power Promotion and Industry Development Act in March and the government’s 55-gigawatt offshore wind auction road map through 2035. It secured a fixed-price contract in the first half of 2026, looking to expand into markets in Japan and other Asia-Pacific countries. “By winning the Taean project following the successful Yeonggwang Nakwol project, we have demonstrated our ability to manufacture and supply large monopiles,” a GS Entec official said. “We will use our accumulated expertise and expanded production capacity to secure more orders in the domestic and overseas offshore wind foundation market.” S.
